questions.q: What is a lock, in the context of SQL Server transactions?
options: The mechanism that controls what other transactions can do with data a transaction is reading or changing
A password required to open a database
A type of index
A synonym for a transaction itself
questions.explain: Locks are the actual implementation behind the Isolation property from Lesson 73.

questions.q: Can multiple transactions hold shared locks on the same data at the same time?
options: Yes — reading doesn't conflict with other reading
No, only one transaction can ever hold a shared lock
Only if they're part of the same session
Shared locks don't exist in SQL Server
questions.explain: This is why many people can SELECT from the same table simultaneously without blocking each other.

questions.q: How many transactions can hold an exclusive lock on the same data at once?
options: Only one
Up to five
An unlimited number, same as shared locks
Exclusive locks don't restrict concurrent access at all
questions.explain: Exclusive locks (for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) prevent other transactions from reading or writing the same data until released.

questions.q: What are the three levels of lock granularity mentioned in this lesson?
options: Row, page, and table
Column, row, and database
Byte, row, and file
Session, transaction, and server
questions.explain: SQL Server automatically chooses granularity based on how much of the table a statement affects.

questions.q: What happens when one transaction needs data that another transaction currently has locked?
options: The second transaction has to wait until the lock is released
The second transaction automatically fails with an error
Both transactions proceed simultaneously without conflict
SQL Server deletes the older transaction's lock automatically
questions.explain: This waiting behavior is exactly what Lesson 75 (Concurrency and Blocking) explores in depth.
